newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWEDEN SAYS NO TO EMU BUT SEEKS TO KEEP DOOR OPEN.
newsitem.headline: SWEDEN SAYS NO TO EMU BUT SEEKS TO KEEP DOOR OPEN.

text.p: Sweden said on Tuesday it would not join the European Union's single currency at its planned launch in 1999 but sought to keep the door open for membership some time in the future.

Prime Minister Goran Persson told a news conference the EU's project for a single currency was too shaky and that public opinion in Sweden, one of the EU's newest recruits, was solidly against membership.
"We are going to hold back on Swedish membership but we are not giving up our room for manoeuvre," Persson said, ending months of Swedish hesitation about whether or not to join EMU.

The Swedish crown firmed on the decision, which markets interpreted as being less negative towards EMU than they had expected. The crown firmed to 4.4860 against the mark from 4.5120 shortly before the decision was announced.
The Stockholm bourse rose after the decision, jumping sharply in the five minutes before the late afternoon close.
Persson said doubts in Sweden about the single currency were so strong that the people would have to be consulted before any decision was taken.
"The question will be settled either through a normal election, a snap poll or through a referendum," he said.
Events in recent weeks in Germany and France had underlined the uncertainty of EMU, Persson said.

In Germany, the government and the Bundesbank have become embroiled in a row over revaluing the country's gold reserves and French commitment to a single currency has been called into question by a Socialist election victory.

The social democratic Swedish prime minister, formerly an avowed supporter of monetary union, said that the situation could change quickly and that Sweden could adhere to EMU before the end of the next parliament, in 2002.
The Centre Party, the Social Democrats' informal coalition partner, said the next scheduled general election in 1998 should be used to determine if Sweden should join EMU.
Market commentators focused on the part of Persson's comments that indicated the door was being kept open for future membership.
PaineWebber economist James Mckay said market reaction had been limited because of its lateness in the European day but the announcement was slightly bullish. "It is a touch more
favourable than the markets thought after the leaks last week. They have not procluded entry over the next few years so people may regard that as favourable for the market."
Midland Bank's Peter Lindqvist said the announcement was in line with his expectations.
"He (Persson) is keeping all doors open which in itself is fairly positive. It is bit of a relief. I think if anything we will see lower yields on the back of this."

JP Morgan's Katharine Hoyland said Persson had been forced to wait for public opinion to turn around. Opinion polls have consistently shown strong dislike for the idea of the Swedish crown being replaced by the euro. "If what we are told is
really all we are seeing right now it implies that, as expected, we are getting the 'no' in 1999 that we have all been braced for but beyond that the jury is essentially still out.

"This is really what I have been expecting. The government would like to retain the flexibility to be able to take the opportunity if the mood swings more into favour than it currently stands," she said. (c) Reuters Limited 1997
